The windows were open, and they were standing at the window. They were watching us, which was also a form of provocation in respect of us who at the moment were lying down face down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Nada Markovska later, and did you maybe discuss testimony here in The Hague together with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never. That was the first time. But I have to tell you something quite interesting. There's very little news concerning your trial, I mean, the trial against Dr. Stakic. I was informed that I would be testifying in the case -- in the Brdjanin case, and the Deutche Welle radio station broadcast a very brief comment on these proceedings. And they mentioned the fact that Nada Markovska had spoken -- had testified in this case. As far as I remember, the reporter, the journalist of Deutche Welle quoted her as saying that she had never seen Stakic in the camp, that she had never seen a single killing in the camp, and that she had only seen occasional beatings which were done by members of some special forces from Banja Luka. Your Honours, Mr. President, I guarantee you with my life, which may sound banal, that if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could the witness be asked to repeat the last sentence. We didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She had never seen Milomir Stakic before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand your answer. Could you please repeat the entire answer once again. It reads on the transcript: "I guarantee you with my life, which may sound banal that if --" and then it stops unfortunately. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. If you had organised a lineup, as you did in my case, for the purposes of identifying Mr. Milomir Stakic, and you had brought in several people including Mr. Milomir Stakic into this courtroom, she would have never identified him. She would have never guessed who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's the time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see each other again.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there's no way I can run away from you, or from fate, it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's neither your fault or my fault. And it's not the fault of Their Honours either. It's the circumstances, I guess. Let me begin with the documents that you were shown by the Prosecutor earlier on today. As far as I understand, you yourself brought these documents today or yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, you always find something in my briefcase.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me -- tell us, please, when you -- when it was that you obtained these documents?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in September last year. Some of it I obtained in September, and some of it I had found even earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit S389.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Five small portions are marked here, all of which were read by you to the Court. However, the main headline in respect of all these texts reads as follows: "Press release." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, it's not the main title; it's part of this war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: War diary, does it refer to the press release? Is it part of the press release of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it contains all of the press releases of the Crisis Staff, and all of these articles are signed "Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the headline "war diary" was given by the journalists, the editor of the paper, or the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess it was given by the editor, and I think I mentioned the fact that -- I mentioned who the editor in chief was at that time, and it was perhaps also upon his recommendation. Milenko Rajlic, who was the right hand of Milomir Stakic, the accused in this case, who had prepared all of these press releases and other people from members of the Crisis Staff. These press releases and these pamphlets were sent to the editor, and they published them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The term "press release," does that mean that the document in question is an order?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To whom were these orders issued, since you say they were orders?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were issued to all people living in the territory of the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it normal for a press release to address the public in general, to address all citizens living in a given area?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I guess that's why it's called "press release" or "public announcement."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when, according to you, the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality was established?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you asked that question several times, Mr. Lukic. Officially, I believe, it was established sometime in May. But let me tell you, I think that the Crisis Staff had been established long time before, but that fact was not made public for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why was it not made public, whereas the establishment of the Serbian Municipality -- the assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor and the executive council were made public? Why wasn't that fact made public as well?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a lot of these things were made public before; but at that time, there was a lot of tension, the atmosphere was such that it eventually led to the takeover. And the reason why they did not mention the fact that the Crisis Staff had been established was because it would have sounded very militant. It would immediately remind the general public of the state of war, which later on turned to be true. You are very well aware of this. When such a decision is made, when the state of war is proclaimed, all valid laws and enactments are declared null and void. And legal decisions are adopted on an ad hoc basis, which can be seen from these press releases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the state of war ever proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... it's better that you have a longer period in time without any interruption to have the break now for the next 20 minutes, until 10 minutes to 6.00. And then you have the time until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And Mr. Lukic, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know you're tired, Mr. Sivac. You have been testifying for the whole day. However, when we stopped, when we interrupted for the break, I asked you if you knew whether the martial law was proclaimed ever.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, as concerns the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, I did read a public announcement once which claimed that martial law had been proclaimed. I think it was signed by Radoslav Brdjanin on behalf of the Crisis Staff of the Krajina region. Now, as Prijedor, after the takeover, formally joined the autonomous region of Banja Luka or Bosanska Krajina, that implied that the same situation applied to Prijedor Municipality too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you wouldn't agree with me if I told you that martial law was only proclaimed in late 1995?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, believe me. Last time I told you that I didn't know much about the legislation, and why retroactively, that means, and why Crisis Staffs had been set up to begin with. You know as well as I do that a Crisis Staff had been set up for the Bosanska Krajina region, I'm talking about the Crisis Staff in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there ever cases in the former Yugoslavia when Crisis Staffs were set up due to floods?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely the problem, Mr. Lukic. We, as a people, and I would like to explain this to the Trial Chamber, very often used the word "staff." Just "staff," like that, without clarifying it. And I'm going to try to explain this now. In the former Yugoslavia, we would set up a staff every time there was a harvest, every time there was some sort of natural calamity. In different situations, different groups of people had different tasks and usually they would call themselves a "staff." However, Mr. Lukic, what we are discussing here is a Crisis Staff. A Crisis Staff, at least I believe so, has a totally different meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This pile of documents that you've brought here today contains a certain document. It's a copy of the Kozarski Vjesnik issue dated the 22nd of May, 1992. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of May? Can you please show me this. It's easier for me to read if I use the large copies. This reads the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could it be, please, put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try and look for it. The 22nd of May, are you referring to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, this is what it looks like, page 3.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it. 22nd of May, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the upper right corner, you have an article. The headline is: "The first session of the Municipal Assembly under the new circumstances." And then the headline continues: "For a more efficient work of the assembly amid war ..." Do you know whether the Municipal Assembly and the Crisis Staff operated at the same time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, as soon as you set up a Crisis Staff, the work of the Municipal Assembly was suspended. I think that's only logical. When a Crisis Staff is set up, new circumstances are created, and the Crisis Staff automatically becomes the biggest body, operative body, in a certain area, in a certain community. And then all decisions of any relevance for that community are made by the Crisis Staff. You can't convene a Municipal Assembly due to extraordinary circumstances, as it says here. It's very difficult to get everyone assembled in one place, all the deputies, and then the procedural matters adopting certain laws and decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and muster some strength to read through this part, about the council.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the one I'm showing you, the one we're talking about. "The first session of the Municipal Assembly under the newly created circumstances," that's the caption. "For more efficient work of the assembly amid war. For the first time in -- since the new situation came about, the deputies of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor came together on Wednesday in order to review a number of questions related to normalising life amid the threat of war. As the president of the assembly, Milomir Stakic said at the beginning of the session: "The war circumstances under which the highest government in the municipality was forced to operate call for greater efficiency by all bodies of the assembly and the assembly itself, but at the same time also a higher level of responsibility of the deputies themselves in making more responsible and better-founded decisions." "As expected, the deputies paid the most attention to decisions on the organisation and operation of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality. The task of the Crisis Staff is to work on coordinating the functions of government to defend the municipal territory, to defend the safety and security of citizens and property, to uphold bodies of government and organise all other areas of life and work. "By coordinating all of the above, the staff makes it possible for the executive committee of the municipality to be a body of legal and executive power and to function as such, as well as to run and organise all the different areas of life. It is seen as particularly important for the Crisis Staff to deal with issues from the purview of the Municipal Assembly, if the assembly is unable to meet. However, the Crisis Staff must send to the Municipal Assembly and show the Municipal Assembly all such decisions as soon as the assembly can meet."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then further down, you have particular decisions concerning taxes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, signed by Ostoja Kresar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why is it that you believe that this decision was published on the 22nd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the reason be that the Crisis Staff was, indeed -- had indeed been set up only several days earlier? Here it reads "Wednesday" and Kozarski Vjesnik usually appears on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me tell you again, I still claim that the Crisis Staff had been set up long before, but it was only made public on as you can see here the 22nd of May. That's as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was any other body aside from the Crisis Staff founded, set up, in secrecy, or was that the only secret body?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the security services, as I said before, as long ago as 1991, they began setting up the security services. And we know from my last testimony who worked on setting up a parallel police force in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that was published in the media?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was never published in the media, as I read just a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But didn't you just a moment ago read that piece where it says that Simo Drljaca was appointed?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, but that was only in May --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm saying April. That was when the takeover took place.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was precisely during that period when the takeover took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So before the takeover, the setting up of the security services was made public, only the Crisis Staff was kept secret?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given you the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As time goes by, you're getting ever more certain that you actually did see Dr. Stakic in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what he was wearing on that particular day, plainclothes, uniform?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plainclothes, civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What exactly did that civilian dress consist of?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was wearing a blue shirt, short-sleeved. Was it white, perhaps? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if he wore a hat or glasses perhaps?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. No, he didn't wear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How well did you actually know Mr. Srdjo Srdic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had known Srdjo Srdic for a very long time. He was my father's friend too. He used to come to my house to see my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you're absolutely certain that Srdjo Srdic was with the delegation on that day in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you describe what Srdjo Srdic was wearing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already pointed out, he was wearing a white suit. And a colleague of mine, Haj Bajic, when he entered Buha and Mujo's room, he told me: "You see Srdjo Srdic over there, he's like the conducter of the Viennes philharmonic orchestra, and he's in a camp visiting us."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Srdic wearing a hat or glasses?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember. Srdjo Srdic never wore glasses or a hat, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How would you describe the personality of Srdjo Srdic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srdjo's biography can easily be divided into two parts: He was a famous dentist in Prijedor. He was an actor with an amateur troupe until I think 1984 or 1985, perhaps even earlier. He was prone to drink, and he was -- he would easily fly into a rage when he was drunk. And later on, as he used to say himself, that was before his cardiac arrest and his health problems, he stopped drinking. And he completely devoted himself to religion. He often went to the orthodox church in Prijedor, although prior to that, he had been a member of the communist league of Yugoslavia for a very long time. I think he was even the president of the local branch at the health centre, the medical centre in Prijedor. That's where he worked. In those years, just before the first democratic elections, he made no secret of being a Serb and a person who liked Serbs. He made no secret of the fact that he had become a nationalist, even if he spent his whole life in Prijedor living alongside with Muslims. It is my submission here that Srdjo Srdic was one of the leaders of the Prijedor Serbs. He was never in the foreground, because he was an elderly person, and his health wasn't very good. He was closely related to -- his wife Milena was a close relative of Radovan Karadzic. That was his second wife, that was very important. Srdjo Srdic's second wife, Milena, she was from Montenegro originally. In the days preceding the first democratic elections, as well as after that, whenever Radovan Karadzic came to Prijedor, he never stayed at a hotel or in any of the public places. Every time he came to Prijedor, he would stay with Srdjo Srdic and his relative Milena. Do you need any further explanations? Do you want me to tell you how many children he has? Because if that's what it takes, I can tell you everything. Srdjo Srdic's son, Misa, married to a Muslim, he's the same age as I am. We were schoolmates at secondary school. Srdjo Srdic did not want to know about his son. He rejected him. And then this son had a step-father, Matija Jakija who was a jeweler from Prijedor; he was a Jew originally from Macedonia. And he married Srdjo's first wife, and the son, Misa. Srdjo Srdic married a Montenegrin woman whose husband, during the 1950s, was some sort of an inform bureau agent in Yugoslavia, but then he was convicted as such, and he was sent to do time in Goli Otok. His last name was Suvarac. When Milena married Srdjo she brought her son from her first marriage. His name was Dragan Suvarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, thank you. Was it conspicuous or was it true that Srdjo Srdic displayed hatred toward Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last period, yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, when I say "in the last period," which period are we referring to exactly?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before the war broke out, in 1990 or thereabouts. I know that he didn't uphold Muslims in very high esteem. I know because once I was in a restaurant, the owner was a Serb, Drago Braco Stupar. We used to go there together sometimes and Srdjo Srdic would also come there. Because just across the way from the restaurant was the only orthodox church in Prijedor. And a number of his friends who were there, and I was there, too, once, they asked him, "Srdjo, how did you end up in all this? You spent your whole life socialising with Muslims." And his reply was: "Yes, the fact which I know with very much regret."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What exactly did he regret?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He regretted having spent the whole of his life with Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Omarska camp, was the Red Cross ever there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Red Cross never brought food or medicines or clothes to the inmates?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please, I'm a serious person. Don't make me laugh here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we'll take it for not true, just in case anyone should claim that it was the case.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we understand each other fairly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show Mr. Sivac the document that we brought today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have an objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. Even without any objections by the Prosecution, ex officio, the Trial Chamber doesn't regard it appropriate to go into details of the intense fear and the health conditions of the witness. And we can't see any relevance based on these documents. And I already guided the Defence before not to touch this issue. There was time enough to discuss this in the absence of the witness, and I extremely regret that we have to discuss this now in the presence of the witness. But may I please hear in addition the submission by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just briefly, for the same reasons and also the fact that this is apparently private material that was obtained from unknown sources. But the main reason is no offer has been made of proof of why it's relevant, and Your Honour previously ruled and there was no offer of proof from the Defence at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the condition of the eyesight or mental state is not important for the recognition of another person, then we can also agree that our evidence is not important for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You start making it more difficult then. I think it's also for the Defence to treat a witness in the appropriate way. And you questioned already the eyesight of the witness earlier, and it was discussed sufficiently. But going now one step further without giving any reason for this, I think you're clearly overstepping. And may I ask, how it is possible, under the rules protecting private data, that you come into the possession of this private data on the witness before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Because I can get it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because I can get this data. Because in my country, I can seek it, request it, and I can get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This data is related to a period of time ending, if I see it correctly, somewhere in 1989. So is it correct that they are not complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what we could get with our limited resources, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It starts in 1980, ends in 1989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it really the case of the Defence that the mental state of the witness before us is an obstacle to the reliability of his testimony? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We think that at that time, when he -- this witness allegedly recognised Dr. Stakic, that it could influence his capability to recognise if he didn't use proper medications, if he is not treated properly in a medical sense. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Submission by the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, as Your Honours know, we were handed this document today. The source of the document is still not identified. Counsel indicated he can legally obtain this, and yet we have no information that these medical records were obtained in a legal manner, no order from a judge or court or authorisation for their release. And simply, still counsel has never made in their written question to the Court -- Ms. Sutherland is handing me a note private session, but I think we've already gone far enough that there's no need at this point -- there has simply never been although the Defence was given a chance by Your Honour to put it in writing any offer of proof that the Defence had any relevant information affecting this witness's credibility. The testimony is clear. This witness had, when he saw Dr. Stakic in the camp, had been detained under horrific conditions, seeing his friends killed in front of him. And undoubtedly, like everyone else in the Omarska camp, was under severe mental stress. That's not disputed by the Prosecution. No relevance from these records from the 1980s has been shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try to take, once again, a pragmatic approach. May I ask you in a very neutral way, and I apologise for doing so. You have seen the source why I proceed this way. Do you ever had the impression that there was a special health condition or a problem with your sight, and maybe glasses, that could be an obstacle, and that would have been an obstacle at that period in time, in 1992, for making clear and undisputable observations about what happened before your detention, during your detention, and after your detention in Omarska? Once again, sorry to have to ask you this question. But please, let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I could see very well, and I needed glasses only for reading, for reading small print. It is true that in everyday life, I often wore sunglasses because my eyes are very sensitive to sunlight which is a kind of occupational disease due to my profession, that is. But my eyesight is perfectly normal. Only when I was reading something did I need glasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever have any special health problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never had anything in particular, apart from certain problems that I had as a result of my work for the security service. I often work at night, so my normal biorhythm was often disrupted. I often had problems with my sleep. As for any other health problems, I don't think that I had anything in particular, apart from the usual problems that everybody has from now and then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does the Defence really want to proceed with their line of questions based on these photocopies we received today? You may discuss this issue with your client.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I be allowed to say something very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This material, has it been provided by the Prijedor medical centre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nobody knows, and I'm more than surprised because it's not only under national legislation, but also under European conventions forbidden without any consent given by a judge to deliver these very sensitive data to third persons. And I'm more than surprised that we received this here in court. And even not knowing what is the source of this -- of these documents, but I don't want to go into details of these legal problems. I only wanted to express my extreme surprise. But the Defence never should say that they had not the possibility to put questions to the witness. And therefore, I'll ask you, and please, if you so want, discuss it together with your client, is it really your case that you want to proceed on that what you started?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I would like first to explain Your Honour, we are talking about Bosnia where foreign troops come and confiscate complete documentation from some institutions. Why would somebody be surprised if we have a few papers? Secondly, to maintain good spirit of this trial, we will not continue with this line of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you feel that there's any kind of prejudice, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours think that there is something confidential, we might go to a private or closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we go into closed session. And then, please, tell us the relevance and the aim of your line of questions, and then we will rule on this, whether the questions are admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us which direction were you facing when the delegation arrived in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was facing east.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to further questions that were already covered or could have been covered in the initial cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] But today, we had extra questions from the Prosecution for a few hours. It's not said that we can only ask questions submitted in written form because of their line of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You covered this area already previously, and now you come back to this area out of context by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because the witness just mentioned -- can we have this discussion without having his headphones in his ears? He can understand, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. so my explanation would be pointless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We don't make now any artificial exercises. If you have any -- I think once again, the Defence should know that there are rules, and they have to obey the rules. And there shouldn't be any abuse of their rights. And we are very close to this once again. So please, what I want to avoid is that the witness before us has to be called once again, and therefore unfortunately I have to allow the question. But please limit it to the absolute necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the visit before noon?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my first testimony that it was around noon. I can't give you the exact time. The specialty of the guards in the camp was to take people a -- watches away and you know that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you wearing sunglasses then?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic, I definitely wasn't. I think your questions are no longer fair, and this is something that I have to point out with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise if you got that impression, because that was never my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you very much, Mr. Sivac, and please forgive me again if we offended you in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the front page of some of the Kozarski Vjesniks that you brought, there appears to be a stamp "Soros media centre." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soros Foundation, the open society.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know where your friend got these Kozarski Vjesniks from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I traced it down to someone from Prijedor who had access to all issues of Kozarski Vjesnik. So this person probably sold this -- sold a number of copies to the Soros library in Sarajevo, the library of the open society in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. I do think we did not mark the one last headline from the 24 July, 1992, article, with the picture of Colonel Arsic reviewing troops. I think perhaps if that could be marked. I believe the next number would be 390B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be on the safe side, may I hear the comments. Is it correct, the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same objections as previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S390B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the other side, Your Honour, we have to propose the document we used from the same Kozarski Vjesnik to be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This would be D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D45B, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any objections. Admitted, D45B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Luckily, it's 7.00, so no time for you to punish me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please understand that I don't answer. This concludes today's hearing. I understand the witness scheduled for today will be here tomorrow at 2.15. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- I'll take it with Judge Agius, this is a problem with this document now and whether it has to be disclosed in the other case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry that this happened. But once again, I don't want to comment on this and whether it's appropriate to act this way by the Defence. So this concludes today's session. And the trial stays adjourned until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of January, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
